title: Floquet Theory and Average Hamiltonian Theory Revisited: Equivalence, Convergence and Applications to NMR
authors: Antonia J. Bock, Matthias Ernst, Götz S. Uhrig
abstract: An accurate theoretical treatment of periodically driven quantum systems is crucial for various fields in the exact sciences, for instance Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Conventionally, either average Hamiltonian theory or Floquet theory is used to predict or describe experimental outcomes, such as the time evolution or the spectra yielding the information of the sample under study. A detailed analysis of the equivalence of these two approaches with an emphasis on applications in NMR will help to improve the theoretical understanding of NMR experiments.   In this work, we identify the Floquet-Magnus expansion as essential to prove the mathematical equivalence of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory. We advocate a calculation scheme which is less prone to algebraic mistakes because explicit integration is avoided. On this basis, we provide the first four orders of both theories. We further examine their applicability to some experiments in NMR. As examples, we investigate the Bloch-Siegert shift and dipolar coupled spin systems under magic-angle spinning.   Based on our analysis, we recommend the use of the Floquet-Van Vleck approach including both the effective Hamiltonian and the kick operator. The consistent separation of secular and non-secular contributions appears to be especially advantageous for numerical robustness. Its accuracy is about three times better than the one provided by average Hamiltonian theory despite their formal equivalence.   Our findings provide important insights into the theoretical background of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory. This includes the extent of their algebraic and perturbative equivalence, with an emphasis on how these findings are of relevance in the analysis of solid-state NMR experiments.
summary: This paper rigorously compares Floquet Theory and Average Hamiltonian Theory for periodically driven quantum systems, using the Floquet-Magnus Expansion to derive higher-order terms for both. The authors conclude that the Floquet-Van Vleck approach is superior for numerical calculations in applications like NMR spectroscopy. It provides a unified theoretical understanding of how these methods relate while offering practical recommendations for implementation.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a detailed mathematical analysis comparing the equivalence, convergence, and practical application of Floquet Theory and Average Hamiltonian Theory (AHT) for periodically driven quantum systems.
main_result: The Floquet-Van Vleck (FVV) approach is recommended over AHT because it is numerically more robust and accurate, despite the formal equivalence of the theories in the infinite limit.
method: The authors utilize the Floquet-Magnus Expansion (FME) to derive systematic, higher-order terms for both AHT and FVV, avoiding explicit time integration.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to periodically driven quantum systems, with a primary focus on Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, modeling the time evolution governed by a time-periodic Hamiltonian H(t).
key_observables: Effective Hamiltonians (F), the kick operator, time evolution operators, and spectroscopic shifts like the Bloch-Siegert shift.
important_parameters: The driving period T, the ratio of driving frequency to system energies, and the order of the perturbation expansion (up to fourth order).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mathematical framework of the Floquet-Magnus expansion and assumes the validity of perturbative expansions in the driving frequency.
figures_summary: Figure 13 shows histograms comparing the relative differences of operators calculated with and without the kick operator for 2-spin and 3-spin MAS systems, highlighting differences between random and MAS Hamiltonians.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the general framework using the FME, derives explicit formulas for higher-order terms in both FVV and AHT, and then validates these formulas and compare their predictions using specific NMR examples like the Bloch-Siegert shift.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, systematic comparison between two cornerstone theoretical tools (AHT and Floquet theory) used to analyze time-periodic quantum dynamics, offering practical guidance on which formalism yields the best numerical results for complex systems like those in NMR.
